name: Karl Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Karl. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions or parties. Everything's confidential. Could you start by telling me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a transmission crew, so the big steel towers, not the street poles. We cover a whole region, so a normal week is three nights in a motel and a lot of driving. A normal day is climbing a tower that's 40 metres up, changing insulators or fitting spacers on the conductors, and getting down before the wind picks up.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the view, honestly, and the money's very good for someone my age. I've already paid off half of a small house and I rent the spare room to a lodger. What wears me out is the motels, the fast food, and missing my mates' birthdays because we're stuck three hours away on a line outage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it out. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it was oversold. Most people I know would say the same. I wouldn't gloat, though, because it'll still be useful for something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means my life stays the same, which is mostly good. I'd like fewer motel nights, but that's nothing to do with AI. Towers don't climb themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going as I am. Pay off the rest of the house in about six years, keep the lodger, and maybe go for a leading hand role in a couple of years. I'd keep my tickets current and that's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any AI tools now, at work or at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. I used one to help write my application for the transmission crew, and I ask it to explain things in the manuals sometimes. It's handy, like a mate who's read everything but has never been up a tower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in your life that worries you, even if AI stays small?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly my back and knees. Old Dennis (the leading hand on my crew) is 54 and he walks like a cowboy. If anything ends my career early, it'll be my joints, not a computer.

say: I'd say AI was **oversold**, without gloating, because it's still useful.
I'd say what most of my **mates** would say anyway.
think: My life **stays the same**, which is mostly good news for me.
I'd like **fewer motel nights**, but that has nothing to do with AI.
do: Pay off the rest of **the house** in about six years.
Keep the **lodger** and keep my tickets current.
Go for a **leading hand** role in a couple of years.
S0.quote: If anything ends my career early, it'll be my joints, not a computer.
fieldNote: Karl's real worry is **physical wear**, set by watching an older crewmate.
He uses AI **occasionally** and practically, without enthusiasm or fear.
He has a clear **money plan**: house, lodger, promotion.

steps.text: Pay off the house mortgage within six years
Apply for a leading hand role in two years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good time to be hands-on. Desk jobs are going to get squeezed, but someone still has to fit the insulators. I'd probably say that a bit too loudly to my cousin who works in insurance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's mostly fine for me, but the crew might change. The drones already fly the lines and take photos, and in this picture the AI reads the photos and decides which towers need work. That means fewer surveyors and planners, and maybe our jobs get planned to the minute.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, but I'd ask to go on the drone and inspection training when the company runs it. That's where the job's heading. And I'd keep the house payments going, nothing changes there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a bit of curiosity. It's not my neck on the line in this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the parts of transmission work that are planning or checking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The line patrol guys, who walk or drive the route looking for damage, they'd be the first to shrink. Some of them would move onto the towers with us, which is fine, more hands. The planning office would get smaller too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the new tools, or wait for others to go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until the first lot of lads had tried them and sorted out the bugs. Then I'd be in, I'm not stubborn about it. I just don't like being the guinea pig on a 40 metre tower.

say: I'd say it's a **good time** to be hands-on while desk jobs get squeezed.
I'd tell my **cousin in insurance** a bit too loudly.
think: The job is **mostly fine** for me, but the crew may change.
AI reading **drone photos** means fewer surveyors and planners, and tighter schedules for us.
do: Ask to join the company's **drone and inspection** training.
Keep the **house payments** going exactly as planned.
Try new tools only **after the first crews** have sorted out the bugs.
S1.quote: The drones already fly the lines and take photos, and in this picture the AI reads the photos and decides which towers need work.
fieldNote: Karl sees change arriving through **drone inspection**, which already exists on his crew.
He expects cuts to **line patrol** and planners, not to climbers.
He'd adopt new tools **after others** test them, true to his steady style.

steps.text: Join the company's drone inspection training when it runs
Keep regular mortgage payments on the house

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's huge and scary, but it'll take longer to reach the towers than people think. Robots on a tower in the wind are a different job from robots in a warehouse. I'd say that, and I'd half believe it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be worried. The planning side goes in 2028 and that's not me, but by 2031 I'm 31, with a house half paid, and the one skill I have is about to be done by machines. Three years isn't long enough to become something else properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd throw everything at the mortgage so the house is clear by 2031. I'd get onto any robot and drone operator course going, because someone has to run the things, at least for a while. If the company offered early redundancy money once robots arrived, I'd look hard at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be the guy who's calm on the outside and checking his bank balance at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When the robots come in 2031, what do you think goes first on a transmission line?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the easy, repeat stuff. A robot crawling along the wire could fit spacers and bird diverters on a long straight line. The tricky jobs, like a damaged tower after a storm, would hang on longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut back on, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Holidays and the new truck I was going to buy. I'd keep the old one running. And I'd stop eating at the motel restaurant, which would probably do my health good anyway.

say: I'd say robots will take **longer to reach** the towers than people think.
I'd point out a tower **in the wind** is different from a warehouse.
think: By **2031** I'd be 31, with a half-paid house and my one skill automated.
Three years is **not long enough** to become something else properly.
do: Put everything into **the mortgage** so the house is clear by 2031.
Take any **robot or drone operator** course the company runs.
Look hard at **early redundancy** money once robots arrive.
feel: **Anxious**, calm outside but checking the bank balance at night.
S2.quote: A robot crawling along the wire could fit spacers and bird diverters on a long straight line.
fieldNote: Karl splits his job into **repeat work** that goes and storm repairs that last longer.
He'd treat a paid-off house as his **safety net** against the robot date.
His public calm hides real **private worry** about having one skill.

steps.text: Make extra mortgage payments to clear the house by 2031
Take the company's robot and drone operator course
Skip the new truck and cut holidays and motel meals
Weigh an early redundancy offer once robots reach towers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to get ready, so let's get ready. I'd push the union rep to get the company talking about it early. I'd say that at the depot, not online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd feel I could get ahead of it. Robots on towers around 2034 means I'd be 35. That's enough time to clear the house and learn the robot side properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the drone course first, then a two-year technical diploma in power systems at night school, so I'm not just a climber. I'd clear the house by about 2032. Then if the robots come, I'm the person who knows both the towers and the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a way I can work with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time change compared with the fast picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big change is the house. In the fast picture I'm racing to pay off my house, and in this one I win the race. And I'd have time to see which jobs the robots really do and which ones they make a mess of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said earlier you'd half believe your own line. Do you believe it more here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit more, yes. With five years you see the robots tried out on real lines before they're on yours. If they struggle with the wind or the storm jobs, everyone will know by then.

say: I'd say there's **time to get ready**, so let's do it.
I'd push the **union rep** to get the company talking early.
think: I could **get ahead** of it, with robots on towers when I'm 35.
There's time to **clear the house** and learn the robot side properly.
do: Do the **drone course**, then a two-year power systems diploma at night school.
Become the person who knows **both towers and machines**.
feel: **Uneasy**, but in a way I can work with.
S3.quote: In the fast picture I'm racing to pay off my house, and in this one I win the race.
fieldNote: For Karl, the extra time mostly means **finishing the mortgage** before robots arrive.
He'd use the gap to **study at night** and become a bridge between towers and machines.
He trusts **seeing robots tested** on other lines before believing the hype.

steps.text: Complete the drone course, then a power systems night diploma
Clear the house mortgage by about 2032
Ask the union rep to raise robot plans with management

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and people should stop panicking. I'd also say that anyone sensible would use the time. That's my usual line on most things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine, I think. Robots around 2039 means I'm 40 with a paid-off house and fifteen years in. I'd still be worried for the young lads coming in, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep climbing, finish the house in six years as planned, and do the diploma at a steady pace. I'd probably try for a leading hand job and then a supervisor job, because supervisors will manage the robot crews. No big leaps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at the back of my mind. Mostly calm day to day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years make you think about a different career altogether?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, around 35. Something like grid control, the people who run the network from the control room, though AI would do a lot of that too. I'd rather stay near the towers and run the crews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mates who aren't in lines work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to look at what their own job is made of. My mate Femi (an accountant) is in more trouble than me in every one of these pictures. Lines work is the one where you get the extra three years.

say: I'd say **ten years is plenty**, so people should stop panicking.
I'd add that anyone sensible would **use the time**.
think: By **2039** I'd be 40, with a paid-off house and fifteen years in.
I'd still worry about the **young apprentices** coming in.
do: Keep climbing and finish **the house** in six years as planned.
Do the **diploma** at a steady pace.
Aim for **supervisor**, since supervisors will run the robot crews.
feel: **Uneasy** at the back of my mind, but mostly calm day to day.
S4.quote: My mate Femi (an accountant) is in more trouble than me in every one of these pictures.
fieldNote: Karl sees the **three-year robot gap** as a real advantage of hands-on work.
His plan is a slow climb to **supervisor**, not a career change.
His worry shifts to the **next generation** of apprentices.

steps.text: Finish paying off the house within six years
Study the power systems diploma part-time
Apply for leading hand, then supervisor roles

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have a half-paid house and one skill when the robots turn up. What would help is the company paying for robot operator training before 2031, and some kind of deal so experienced climbers get first go at those jobs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Who's responsible when things go wrong. Somebody has to sign for the work when a robot drops a conductor on a road, and that's where people like me will stay useful longest. Signing off and taking the blame.

headlineQuote: Somebody has to sign for the work when a robot drops a conductor on a road, and that's where people like me will stay useful longest.
portrait: Karl is a 27-year-old **transmission lineworker** who climbs steel towers and spends three nights a week in motels.
He's half paid off **a small house** and rents a room to a lodger.
He uses AI **now and then**, and adopts new tools once colleagues have tested them.
He worries most when robots arrive **soon after 2028**, before his house is clear.
With more time he plans **night study** and a move toward supervising robot crews.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with robots arriving while he still has a mortgage and one skill.
whatWouldHelp: First go at those jobs for **experienced climbers**.
